paraphrase: Rāmānuja prays that his understanding may take the form of devotion (bhakti) to the supreme Brahman, Śrīnivāsa (in whom Śrī dwells), whose play is the creation, maintenance and dissolution of all worlds, whose one vow is to protect the hosts of beings who bow to him, and who shines in the crown of the Veda (the Upaniṣads).

original.text: akhila-bhuvana-janma-sthema-bhaṅgādi-līle vinata-vividha-bhūta-vrāta-rakṣaika-dīkṣe | śruti-śirasi vidīpte brahmaṇi śrīnivāse bhavatu mama parasmin śemuṣī bhakti-rūpā ||
original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The extensive commentary (vṛtti) on the Brahma Sūtras composed by the venerable Bodhāyana was abridged by earlier teachers; following their view, Rāmānuja will explain the words of the sūtras.
notes: Bodhāyana's Vṛtti: src:bodhayana-vrtti (U13), lost.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: 'Then' (atha) means after the inquiry into ritual action (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā) has been completed, because the knowledge that the fruits of ritual are small and impermanent gives rise to the desire to know Brahman; the two Mīmāṃsās form a single science (śāstra).
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The knowledge that the Upaniṣads enjoin for liberation is not the understanding of a sentence but meditation (dhyāna, upāsana): a steady, unbroken remembrance (dhruvānusmṛti) like a stream of oil, repeated until it becomes as vivid as direct perception (darśana-samānākāra); this remembrance, being supremely dear, is bhakti, and the Lord chooses and reveals himself to the one who is dearest to him ('whom he chooses, by him he is attained').
notes: Cites Chāndogya 7.26.2 ('dhruvā smṛtiḥ'), Muṇḍaka 2.2.8 and Kaṭha 1.2.23 / Muṇḍaka 3.2.3.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Following the Vākyakāra, such meditation is attained through seven aids: discrimination (viveka) in food, freedom from desire (vimoka), repeated practice (abhyāsa), performance of the ritual duties (kriyā), virtues (kalyāṇa: truthfulness, uprightness, compassion, generosity, non-injury, non-covetousness), freedom from dejection (anavasāda) and from excessive elation (anuddharṣa).
notes: The Vākyakāra is identified by the tradition with Ṭaṅka (Brahmanandin).
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The great prior view (mahāpūrvapakṣa), stated by Rāmānuja on behalf of the Advaitins: Brahman is pure, undifferentiated consciousness; all difference — knower, known, the plurality of selves and the world — is projected by a beginningless avidyā that is neither real nor unreal, and is removed by the knowledge of identity arising from texts such as 'tat tvam asi'.
notes: Opponent's view as reported by Rāmānuja in the Śrībhāṣya (reporting source: src:sribhasya).
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: No means of knowledge establishes an undifferentiated object: perception, even at its first, non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) moment, grasps an object with some distinguishing feature; inference rests on perception; and scripture, made of words with stems and suffixes, conveys only qualified meanings. Hence Brahman is qualified (saviśeṣa).
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Consciousness (anubhūti) is not the self: it belongs to someone and is of something, arises and ceases as an attribute; the self is the knower that appears as 'I', and this 'I' persists in deep sleep and in liberation.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Avidyā as the Advaitins conceive it is untenable in seven ways (saptavidha-anupapatti): it has no possible locus (āśraya), cannot conceal self-luminous Brahman (tirodhāna), has no coherent nature (svarūpa), cannot be 'indescribable' (anirvacanīya), has no means of knowledge proving it (pramāṇa), has no possible remover (nivartaka), and cannot be removed (nivṛtti).
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: All cognition is of the real (satkhyāti, 'yathārthaṃ sarvavijñānam'): even in the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl, silver-particles are really present, since by the scriptural triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) every substance contains the others; error is partial grasp, not the appearance of the unreal.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Bondage is caused by karma, which is what scripture calls avidyā ('the third power, called avidyā-karma', Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.61); it contracts the self's knowledge. It is ended not by a knowledge of identity but by meditation pleasing to the Lord, who, gratified, releases the soul.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: 'That from which the origin, etc., of this (world) proceed' defines Brahman: the cause of the world's origin, maintenance and dissolution, which implies omniscience, omnipotence and the other auspicious qualities.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Brahman is known only from scripture (śāstrayonitvāt): inference cannot prove a single omniscient maker of the world, since for every argument from effects a counter-argument can be made; the Lord is established by the Veda alone.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The Upaniṣads have Brahman as their consistent purport (samanvaya); they are authoritative about an existent reality and are not merely subsidiary to injunctions to act.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The self 'consisting of bliss' (ānandamaya) of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad is the supreme Brahman itself, because of the repeated mention of bliss.
notes: Sūtra number follows Rāmānuja's division as recalled; his numbering can differ by one or two from Śaṅkara's — check.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The inner controller (antaryāmin) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka — who dwells in earth, the elements and the self, whom they do not know, whose body they are, and who controls them from within — is the supreme Self, not the individual soul or pradhāna; this text shows all things, including selves, to be Brahman's body.
notes: Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa of BS 1.2; chapter-level ref, sūtra numbers not given. The Mādhyandina reading 'yasyātmā śarīram' is central.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Brahman is the material cause (prakṛti) as well as the efficient cause, for only so do the promise 'by knowing one, all is known' and the example of clay hold; Brahman with souls and matter in their subtle state as its body becomes, with them in gross state, the world.
notes: Sūtra number follows Rāmānuja's division as recalled; his numbering can differ by one or two from Śaṅkara's — check.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Definition of body (śarīra): any substance that a conscious being can wholly control and support for its own purposes, and whose essential nature is to be subservient (śeṣa) to it, is that being's body; in this sense all souls and all matter are the body of the Lord.
notes: Sūtra number follows Rāmānuja's division as recalled; his numbering can differ by one or two from Śaṅkara's — check.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The world as effect is non-different from Brahman its cause (tad-ananyatvam), as pots are clay; but the effect is a real state of the cause, and 'names and forms' are real — the passage does not declare the world false.
notes: Ārambhaṇa-adhikaraṇa; Sūtra number follows Rāmānuja's division as recalled; his numbering can differ by one or two from Śaṅkara's — check.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The individual self is not produced but eternal; it is by nature a knower (jñātṛ), not mere knowledge; it is atomic (aṇu) in size, yet its attributive consciousness spreads through the body as the light of a lamp fills a room.
notes: BS 2.3 (sūtras on the self's eternity, knowership and atomicity); chapter-level ref.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The self is an agent (kartṛ), else injunctions would be pointless; but its agency depends on the supreme Self, who, taking into account the self's first effort, grants consent (anumati), so that the self remains answerable.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The self is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman — not a piece cut off, but as an attribute (viśeṣaṇa) is part of what it qualifies, like the light of a luminary or the body of an embodied being; hence both difference and non-difference texts are true.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Even though it abides in bodies and places, the supreme Brahman is not touched by their defects: everywhere scripture gives it a twofold mark (ubhaya-liṅga) — freedom from every imperfection and possession of all auspicious qualities.
notes: BS 3.2.11 ('na sthānato 'pi parasyobhayaliṅgaṃ sarvatra hi'); chapter-level ref.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: 'Not so, not so' (neti neti) negates only the limitation — that Brahman is merely 'so much' as the forms just described — for the text goes on to say more ('the real of the real'); it does not negate Brahman's qualities.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The objects seen in dream are created by the Lord himself to give the dreamer the fruits of minor karma; they are real for the dreamer, though lasting only for the dream.
notes: BS 3.2.1–6; recalled, check.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: In deep sleep the self rests in the supreme Self within the heart and its channels; its knowledge is contracted, but the self persists as the 'I', as shown by the later recollection 'I slept happily'.
notes: BS 3.2.7ff.; recalled, check.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The meditation that liberates must be repeated, not done once, and continued daily until death, with the Lord meditated upon as the meditator's own self.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: When Brahman is attained through meditation, earlier sins are destroyed and later ones do not cling (uttara-pūrvāghayor aśleṣa-vināśau); merit is similarly shed; only the karma that has begun to bear fruit (prārabdha) remains until the body falls.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: At death the knower of Brahman departs through the channel in the head (the hundred-and-first), the heart's opening being lit up by the grace of the Lord dwelling there.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The liberated soul travels by the path beginning with light (arcirādi) — flame, day, the bright fortnight, the northern course, the year, wind, sun, moon, lightning — and is then led by superhuman escorts (ātivāhika) to Brahman; the path is for all who meditate on Brahman.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Reaching the highest light, the self manifests its own true nature (svena rūpeṇa abhiniṣpadyate), freed from karma; it experiences itself as inseparable from Brahman, being its mode, and enjoys Brahman with all his qualities.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The released self attains equality with Brahman in enjoyment and in all powers except the cosmic functions of creating, sustaining and ruling the world (jagad-vyāpāra-varjam), which belong to the Lord alone.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: There is no return for the released soul, on the word of scripture ('he does not return, he does not return').
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Homage to Viṣṇu, the master (śeṣin) of all sentient and insentient things, who reclines on Śeṣa, the treasury of spotless, infinite auspicious qualities.

original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Rāmānuja

location.ref: opening prose (the purport of the Upaniṣads)

paraphrase: The purport of the Upaniṣads is this: meditation on, worship of and prostration to the feet of the supreme Person, which is exceedingly dear, preceded by true knowledge of the individual and the supreme self and accompanied by the duties of one's class and stage of life, and whose fruit is attaining him.
notes: Paragraph number not given (the common numbering was not recalled with certainty).
speaker: Rāmānuja

location.ref: section on the three kinds of scriptural text

paraphrase: Scripture has texts of difference (bheda-śruti), texts of non-difference (abheda-śruti) and mediating texts (ghaṭaka-śruti) such as the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa and the Subāla Upaniṣad, which declare souls and matter to be the Lord's body; through the body–self relation all three are true together, without rejecting any.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: In 'tat tvam asi' both words denote Brahman: 'that' denotes Brahman as the omniscient cause of the world, 'you' denotes Brahman having the individual soul as its body; co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of two words with different grounds (pravṛtti-nimitta) in one object — without giving up their primary meanings — teaches Brahman as qualified, not an attributeless identity.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Rāmānuja rejects three rival readings of the Upaniṣads: that of Śaṅkara (Brahman, pure consciousness, is covered by avidyā), of Bhāskara (Brahman itself is bound by real limiting adjuncts) and of Yādavaprakāśa (Brahman itself transforms into souls and matter); each makes Brahman the seat of ignorance, bondage or change.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The Chāndogya's description of the golden Person's eyes as 'kapyāsa' lotuses means lotuses opened by the sun (the one who drinks water), not something ignoble; the Lord's form is supremely beautiful, and descriptions of his form are to be read so.
notes: Hagiographies connect this reading with Rāmānuja's break with Yādavaprakāśa.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme Brahman: texts such as 'Nārāyaṇa alone existed, not Brahmā nor Īśāna' show that Brahmā and Śiva are individual souls, parts of his body, who hold office by his grant.
speaker: Rāmānuja

location.ref: section on bhakti as the means

paraphrase: The means to reach the Lord is bhakti — knowledge that has taken the form of love (prīti) — which is born of karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga performed as his worship, and which is won through his grace.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, opposed to all evil and the sole abode of auspicious qualities, beyond the reach of Brahmā and the gods, descended as Kṛṣṇa to be accessible to all; in the Gītā, using Arjuna as occasion, he teaches bhakti-yoga, prepared by karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The Lord declares that he, Arjuna and the kings never were not and never will not be: the plurality of eternal selves is real and taught by the Lord who knows the highest truth, and so is not due to ignorance or adjuncts.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Karma-yoga, which includes knowledge of the self and is free of the risk of lapse, is by itself a sufficient means to the vision of the self (ātmāvalokana), even for those fit for jñāna-yoga.
notes: Chapter-level ref (Gītā ch. 3); verse not recalled.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: One who knows the Lord's birth and acts to be divine — not caused by karma, taken by his own will in a body of pure sattva, for protecting the good — is not reborn after death but comes to him.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Four kinds of virtuous people worship the Lord — the distressed seeking lost wealth, the seeker of wealth, the seeker of the self (kaivalya), and the wise one (jñānī) who seeks him alone; the wise one is dearest and is, the Lord says, his very self, for he cannot sustain himself without him.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Those of low birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras too reach the highest goal by taking refuge in the Lord.
notes: Rāmānuja's gloss on Gītā 9.32 as recalled.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: 'Know me also as the knower of the field in all fields': the Lord is the self of all knowers, who are his body; hence co-referential statements name the embodied soul together with the Lord its self.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: There are three persons: the perishable (bound souls, joined with matter), the imperishable (released souls), and the supreme Person (Puruṣottama), distinct from both, who pervades and supports the three worlds.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: True relinquishment (tyāga) in action is to give up the sense that one is the agent, the sense that the act is one's own, and desire for its fruit, regarding the Lord as the agent and the owner; relinquishing the acts themselves is not meant.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Rāmānuja gives two readings of 'abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone': (1) perform karma-, jñāna- and bhakti-yoga while abandoning the sense of agency, ownership and fruit, taking the Lord alone as the agent, object and means; (2) for one who feels unable to begin bhakti-yoga because of the sins obstructing it, or through lack of qualification, take refuge in the Lord in place of the expiations and he will free you from those sins — do not grieve.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Homage to the sage Nāthamuni, a mass of inconceivable, wonderful, effortless knowledge and dispassion, an ocean of deep devotion to the Lord.

original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: Yāmuna bows his head to the glorious feet, lovely with vakula flowers, of the first head of our clan (Nammāḻvār), which are for all his descendants mother, father, wives, children and wealth — everything.

original.text: mātā pitā yuvatayas tanayā vibhūtiḥ sarvaṃ yad eva niyamena mad-anvayānām | ādyasya naḥ kulapater vakulābhirāmaṃ śrīmat tad-aṅghri-yugalaṃ praṇamāmi mūrdhnā ||
original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: 'I am not established in dharma, nor a knower of the self, nor have I devotion to your lotus feet; having nothing (akiñcana), with no other refuge, O refuge of all, I take refuge at the root of your feet.'

original.text: na dharma-niṣṭho 'smi na cātma-vedī na bhaktimāṃs tvac-caraṇāravinde | akiñcano 'nanya-gatiḥ śaraṇya tvat-pāda-mūlaṃ śaraṇaṃ prapadye ||
original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: Addressed to Śrī: your lover is the supreme Person, the serpent-king your couch and seat, Garuḍa (the Veda embodied) your mount, world-enchanting māyā your curtain, the gods from Brahmā and Śiva down with their consorts your servants and maids — 'Śrī' alone is your name; how can we praise you?

original.text: kāntas te puruṣottamaḥ phaṇipatiḥ śayyāsanaṃ vāhanaṃ vedātmā vihageśvaro yavanikā māyā jagan-mohinī | brahmeśādi-sura-vrajaḥ sa-dayitas tvad-dāsa-dāsī-gaṇaḥ śrīr ity eva ca nāma te bhagavati brūmaḥ kathaṃ tvāṃ vayam ||
original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: Even the Lord, her beloved, cannot measure the boundless greatness of Śrī, as he cannot measure his own; she is ever in accord with him.
notes: Verse number and wording recalled with low confidence.
speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: The self is distinct from the body, the senses, the mind, the vital breath and cognition; it is established in the awareness 'I', is self-luminous, eternal, atomic and many, and is the knower of its cognitions.
speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: Against the Advaitins, consciousness without subject or object is never found; consciousness is always someone's and of something, and the non-dual texts do not deny the plurality of real things.
notes: The Saṃvitsiddhi survives in part; content recalled from citations.
speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: Yāmuna argues for the existence of a Lord who is the maker of the world; whether he accepts the Naiyāyika inference or rests the proof on scripture alone (as Rāmānuja does) is not settled from memory here.
notes: Low confidence on Yāmuna's exact stance; check the text.
speaker: Yāmuna

paraphrase: Rāmānuja first takes refuge in Śrī — whose form, qualities and glory befit the Lord's delight, who is inseparable from him, the mother of all, who teaches the good of the whole world — as his refuge (the mediator), before approaching Nārāyaṇa.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: Having recited the Lord's infinite auspicious qualities and confessed his own countless offences, Rāmānuja, with no other refuge, takes refuge at the Lord's feet and asks for supreme devotion, supreme knowledge and supreme love (parabhakti, parajñāna, paramabhakti) and for eternal service.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The Lord replies that by his grace all this is granted: the refugee's sins are gone, he will attain the Lord's service at the end of this body; let him have no doubt, and dwell happily at Śrīraṅgam, reciting the dvaya with its meaning, until the body falls.
speaker: the Lord (as recorded by Rāmānuja)

paraphrase: Rāmānuja surrenders himself to Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam and prays to become his eternal servant, whose one joy is service according to the Lord's pleasure.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: One who has surrendered by the Lord's grace should meditate on Vaikuṇṭha — its divine city and hall, the Lord seated with Śrī, Bhū and Nīlā, the eternal servants (nityasūris) ever serving him — and long to join that service.
speaker: Rāmānuja

paraphrase: The Nityagrantha lays down the daily worship of the Lord at home for the surrendered: purifications, meditation on the teacher lineage, worship of the Lord's image with offerings, recitation and prostration, all done as service without desire for fruit.
notes: Summary of the whole manual, recalled.

paraphrase: Nāthamuni, hearing the Tiruvāymoḻi decad ending 'these ten of the thousand', sought the whole; at Kurukūr he recited Madhurakavi's Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu twelve thousand times and Nammāḻvār appeared to him and gave him all four thousand hymns with their meanings, which he arranged and set to music.

When Yāmuna died before Rāmānuja could meet him, three fingers of his hand remained folded; Rāmānuja vowed to write a commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, to honour Parāśara and Vyāsa, and to honour Nammāḻvār, and the fingers unfolded.

After making Rāmānuja come eighteen times, Tirukkōṭṭiyūr Nambi taught him the secret meaning of the tirumantra, charging him to keep it secret; Rāmānuja proclaimed it to all from the temple tower, saying that if he went to hell for disobedience, so many would be saved, and his teacher embraced him as 'Emperumāṉār'.

Through Tirukkacci Nambi, Varadarāja of Kāñcī answered Rāmānuja's doubts with six sayings: I am the supreme reality; difference is the true doctrine; surrender (prapatti) is the means; the surrendered need no last remembrance at death; liberation follows at the end of this body; take Periya Nambi as your teacher.
speaker: Varadarāja (through Tirukkacci Nambi)

paraphrase: When a Cōḻa king demanded that Rāmānuja sign that nothing is higher than Śiva, Kūreśa went in his teacher's place, disguised, refused, and was blinded; Periya Nambi, taken with him, died.

The Advaita renouncer Yajñamūrti debated Rāmānuja at Śrīraṅgam for eighteen days; on the eighteenth, after Rāmānuja prayed to the Lord, he conceded and became Rāmānuja's disciple as Aruḷāḷa Perumāḷ Emperumāṉār.

When Maṇavāḷa Māmuni completed a year's exposition of the Īṭu before Raṅganātha, the Lord, appearing as a child, recited: 'I bow to the sage Ramyajāmātṛ, object of the grace of Śrīśaileśa, ocean of wisdom, devotion and other virtues, devoted to Yatīndra (Rāmānuja).'

original.text: śrīśaileśa-dayāpātraṃ dhī-bhakty-ādi-guṇārṇavam | yatīndra-pravaṇaṃ vande ramya-jāmātaraṃ munim ||
original.edition: wording as commonly recited in the tradition; recalled from memory, not yet checked against an edition

speaker: Raṅganātha (the tradition's account)

paraphrase: On Tiruvāymoḻi 6.10.10 ('I cannot bear to part even for a moment,' says she of the lotus, dwelling on your chest), the commentary reads Nammāḻvār's taking refuge at Tirumala as surrender to the Lord's feet with Śrī, ever on his chest, as mediator — the meaning of the dvaya.
notes: Commentarial reading recalled in outline only.

paraphrase: The supreme deity is Nārāyaṇa together with Śrī: the two are inseparable, and the divine couple (mithuna) is the object of worship, the refuge and the goal; Brahmā, Rudra and the other gods are souls in his body.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Prapatti is for those who, lacking the knowledge, ability or patience for bhakti-yoga, or being barred from it by birth, have no other means (ākiñcanya) and seek no other refuge (ananyagatitva); it is open to all, of every class.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Prapatti is an independent means (svatantra-upāya) to liberation, not a limb of bhakti; performed once, it achieves what bhakti-yoga achieves; the Lord, already accomplished (siddhopāya), is the one who grants, and the surrender is the means that is performed (sādhyopāya) and the occasion (vyāja) of his grace.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Prapatti has five limbs — the resolve to do what pleases the Lord (ānukūlya-saṅkalpa), avoidance of what displeases him (prātikūlya-varjana), great faith that he will protect (mahāviśvāsa), choosing him as protector (goptṛtva-varaṇa) and helpless humility (kārpaṇya) — with the principal act (aṅgin), laying down the burden of one's protection at his feet (ātma-nikṣepa, bharanyāsa).
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given. Based on the six-fold śaraṇāgati verse of the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā 37 / Lakṣmī Tantra 17.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Surrender with its limbs may be performed by oneself (svaniṣṭha), by repeating the words after the teacher (uktiniṣṭha), or by the teacher on one's behalf (ācāryaniṣṭha); in each case it is done once, with the sense that even this act is done by the Lord's grace and for his sake.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Once prapatti is done the surrendered has done all that is to be done for liberation (kṛtakṛtya); he is free of anxiety about his salvation and lives in service while the body lasts.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: After surrender, the obligatory and occasional duties of scripture must still be performed — as the Lord's command (ājñā) and as service, not as means; omitting them offends the Lord; in addition there are services done by his permission (anujñā).
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Offences committed unknowingly after surrender do not cling; for deliberate offences the surrendered must make expiation or repeat surrender as expiation, else the Lord corrects him by light punishment in this life, without cancelling liberation.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: At death the Lord himself leads the surrendered soul out through the channel of the head; the surrendered need not achieve a last remembrance, for the Lord remembers him; the distressed surrenderer (ārta) is freed at the end of this body, the patient one (dṛpta) when his begun karma is spent.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: In Vaikuṇṭha the freed soul, its knowledge fully expanded, enjoys the whole Brahman with all his qualities and glories, and that enjoyment overflows as service (kainkarya) in all places and at all times.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The tirumantra (oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya): the praṇava declares that the soul belongs to the Lord alone; 'namaḥ' that it does not belong to itself; 'nārāyaṇāya' asks for service to Nārāyaṇa, the abode of all souls and the one in whom all abide.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The dvaya: its first half is the act of surrender — 'I take refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa, who is with Śrī'; its second half is the prayer for the goal — 'to Nārāyaṇa with Śrī, obeisance', i.e. service to the divine couple free of self-interest.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The carama-śloka (Gītā 18.66): the Lord bids the one unable to follow other means to give them up and take him alone as the means through surrender; he will free him from all sins; he should not grieve. The surrender it enjoins is itself the means that is to be performed.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: A true teacher (sadācārya) teaches out of compassion alone, without seeking gain, the doctrine received through the unbroken line; the disciple tests and approaches him with humility, serves him, keeps the teaching and hands it on only to the fit.
notes: Chapter (adhikāra) named as recalled; chapter number not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The Jīva section: the soul is eternal, atomic, self-luminous as 'I', a knower having attributive consciousness that contracts and expands, many in number; it is not the body, senses or mind.
notes: Section (sara) 2, Jīvasara; verse numbers not given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The Nāyaka section: the Lord, qualified by souls and matter, is the one cause of the world, with infinite auspicious qualities; the rival accounts of God (Advaita's, Nyāya's) are refuted.
notes: Section (sara) 3, Nāyakasara.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is impossible: while the body lasts, karma and bondage remain, and scripture places release after the body falls; the Advaitin's 'liberated-while-living' is still bound.
notes: Vāda number not recalled.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The wise should offer the self saying: 'I myself, the burden of my protection, and the fruit of that protection are not mine but belong to the Lord of Śrī alone.'
notes: The verse 'ahaṃ mad-rakṣaṇa-bharo mad-rakṣaṇa-phalaṃ tathā / na mama śrīpater eva...' — verse 1 or 2; wording not certain, so no original given.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The sandals (pādukā) of Raṅganātha are praised as Śaṭhakopa (Nammāḻvār) and as the teacher who, like Bharata's sandals ruling Ayodhyā, brings the Lord to those who cannot reach him.
notes: Summary of the opening section; verse numbers not given.

paraphrase: Nine steps lead to the supreme abode: discrimination (viveka), disgust with saṃsāra (nirveda), dispassion (virakti), fear of rebirth (bhīti), winning the Lord's favour through surrender (prasādana), departure from the body (utkramaṇa), the path of light (arcirādi), arrival in the divine realm (divyadeśa-prāpti) and attainment (prāpti).
notes: Names of the nine steps recalled; check the text.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The Mīmāṃsā of ritual and the Mīmāṃsā of Brahman are one science with one purport; rightly read, the ritual texts presuppose the Lord as the one worshipped in all rites and the giver of their fruits.
notes: Ref to the opening sūtra; exact location unchecked.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Prapatti (nikṣepa) is taught by scripture — the Upaniṣads, Itihāsas, Purāṇas and Pāñcarātra — as an independent means to liberation, and the objections that it is not a means, or not a proper Vedic practice, are answered.
notes: Summary of the whole work; ref coarse.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Commenting on Yāmuna's Catuḥślokī, Deśika argues that Śrī, like the Lord, is all-pervading and his equal in lordship, a co-refuge and co-goal, while remaining dependent on him as his consort.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: Deśika declines the patronage of kings: his wealth is the Lord (Varadarāja) alone, inherited from his forebears; he will not praise the rich for a living.
speaker: Vedānta Deśika

paraphrase: The tirumantra: 'oṃ' shows the soul to be the Lord's alone (ananyārha-śeṣatva); 'namaḥ' removes the sense of belonging to oneself and of being one's own means; 'nārāyaṇāya' is the prayer for service to Nārāyaṇa in all states.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The dvaya: the first half shows Śrī as mediator (puruṣakāra) and the Lord's feet, with his qualities of motherly love (vātsalya), lordship (svāmitva), gracious condescension (sauśīlya) and accessibility (saulabhya), as the means; the second half is the prayer for service to the divine couple, removing any sense that the service is for oneself.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The carama-śloka: 'abandoning all dharmas' means giving up every other means, including the idea that one's own surrender is a means; 'me alone' means the Lord himself, already accomplished, is the only means; 'do not grieve' — all burden is his.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Śrī's mediation (puruṣakāra): in separation and in union she turns the soul toward the Lord and the Lord toward the soul — the soul by her grace, the Lord by her beauty — as shown by Sītā's intercession even for those who wronged her.
notes: Prakaraṇa numbering as in Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's division, recalled with low confidence; aphorism numbers not given.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The glory of the means: the Lord himself is the means; surrender (prapatti) is not a means but the soul's acceptance fitting its nature, and to regard it as a means would make it one more act of one's own; the means is 'already accomplished' (siddha).
notes: Prakaraṇa numbering as in Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's division, recalled with low confidence; aphorism numbers not given.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The Lord does not merely overlook the faults of those who come to him but relishes them (doṣa-bhogya), as a cow licks the dirt from its newborn calf, out of motherly love (vātsalya).
notes: Prakaraṇa numbering as in Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's division, recalled with low confidence; aphorism numbers not given.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The Lord's grace is without cause (nirhetuka): he saves by his own will; the soul's surrender is not what earns it.
notes: Prakaraṇa numbering as in Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's division, recalled with low confidence; aphorism numbers not given.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The conduct of the surrendered: to avoid offence against the Lord, against his devotees (bhāgavata-apacāra — the gravest, including judging devotees by birth) and the unbearable offence (asahya-apacāra); to serve devotees; to keep scriptural conduct as service and for the example of the world.
notes: Prakaraṇa numbering as in Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's division, recalled with low confidence; aphorism numbers not given.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Finally, for one who can do nothing, the gracious regard of the teacher (ācārya-abhimāna) is itself what saves: to be held as his own by a true teacher is the last refuge.
notes: Prakaraṇa numbering as in Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's division, recalled with low confidence; aphorism numbers not given.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Cit: the soul is distinct from body, senses, mind, breath and intellect; it is self-luminous, blissful, eternal, atomic, imperceptible, unthinkable, partless, unchanging, the substrate of knowledge, controlled, supported and owned by the Lord; souls are bound, freed or eternal.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Acit: insentient reality is of three kinds — pure sattva (the substance of Vaikuṇṭha and the Lord's forms), mixed sattva (prakṛti with the three guṇas, the stuff of bodies and worlds) and that devoid of sattva (time).
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Īśvara: the Lord is opposed to all evil and has infinite auspicious qualities; he is the cause of the world, its self and support, present in five forms — the supreme, the vyūhas, the descents, the inner controller and the image.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Five things must be known, each fivefold: the self (eternal, freed, bound, isolated and seeking release), the Lord (supreme, vyūha, descent, inner controller, image), the means (karma, jñāna, bhakti, prapatti, the teacher's regard), the goal (dharma, wealth, pleasure, self-enjoyment, the Lord's service) and the obstacles (to right knowledge of the self, of the Lord's supremacy, of the means, of the goal, and to attainment).
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The surrendered soul, leaving the body, is led by the Lord along the path of light through the worlds of the escorting deities, crosses the Virajā river, sheds the subtle body, receives a divine form and is welcomed in Vaikuṇṭha to eternal service.
notes: Summary of the whole work; recalled in outline.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: The tirumantra contains nine relations between the Lord and the soul: father and son, protector and protected, master (śeṣin) and servant, husband and wife, knower and known, owner and owned, support and supported, self and body, enjoyer and enjoyed.
notes: The nine are also listed in the verse 'pitā ca rakṣakaḥ śeṣī bhartā jñeyo ramāpatiḥ…'; attribution of this short work recalled with low confidence.
speaker: Piḷḷai Lokācārya

paraphrase: Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi is the essence of the four Vedas in Tamil; the Tamil Veda, uttered by one born outside the brahmin class, is equal in authority to the Sanskrit and reveals its heart.
notes: Summary of the work's theme; aphorism numbers not given.

paraphrase: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni recounts the Āḻvārs and the commentaries on their hymns and urges the faithful to hold to the teacher lineage and the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam.
notes: Summary of the whole work.

paraphrase: There are three means of valid knowledge — perception, inference and scripture; comparison and the rest are included in these; all valid cognition is of the real.

Reality is substance (dravya) or non-substance (adravya). The six substances are prakṛti, time, pure sattva (the eternal realm), attributive consciousness, the soul and the Lord; the ten non-substances are the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), the five sense qualities (sound, touch, form, taste, smell), conjunction and potency (śakti).

Souls are bound, freed or eternal; bound souls seek enjoyment or liberation; seekers of liberation seek either isolation of the self (kaivalya) or the Lord; seekers of the Lord are devotees (bhakta) or the surrendered (prapanna).
notes: Chapter (avatāra) number recalled with low confidence.

paraphrase: The Lord has five forms: the supreme (para) in Vaikuṇṭha; the four vyūhas (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha), each manifesting pairs of the six qualities for creation, maintenance, dissolution and for meditation; the descents; the inner controller; and the image (arcā).
notes: Chapter number recalled with low confidence.
